title: showtime
aim: Explore festivals, performing, film and music, and learn to emphasise ideas and speak vaguely.
objectives: Describe festivals and explain how events can be sustainable
Talk about performing and focus attention with cleft sentences
Recommend films and series using vague language
Discuss music tastes and write a forum comment

lessons.title: Festival
goals: Use defining and non-defining relative clauses
Plan an eco-friendly festival and write a formal proposal

grammar.title: Relative clauses
grammar.shortAr: جمل الموصول: تعريفية بلا فواصل، وغير تعريفية بين فاصلتين
points: Defining relative clauses identify which person or thing you mean; no commas are used.
Use who/that for people, which/that for things, whose for possession, where for places and when for times.
Non-defining clauses add extra information, take commas, and cannot use that or omit the pronoun.
In informal English prepositions end the clause; in formal English they may come before whom or which.
table: The festival-goers who arrived by bus saved time.
It is a venue where people can camp.
The wood (which) they reused was local.
Green Man, which began in 2003, is very popular.
The organiser to whom I spoke was helpful.
exceptions: Never use that in a non-defining relative clause.
Do not repeat the noun after the relative pronoun.
The relative pronoun cannot be omitted when it is the subject.

vocab.example: Festival-goers are encouraged to take their rubbish home.
The festival moved to a larger venue by the river.
The organisers want to cut waste this year.
Several performers cancelled because of the heat.
Thousands of people attend the event each summer.
The line-up includes local bands and guest acts.
Good food and live music attract big crowds.
The relaxed atmosphere makes the festival special.
The organisers aim to run a sustainable event.

reading.summary: An article presents festivals as enjoyable but wasteful, mentioning plastic cups, abandoned tents and carbon emissions, and points to sustainable events as an alternative. A second text describes Burning Man's art, gift economy and 'leave no trace' policy.

listening.summary: Introductory listening linked to festival vocabulary.
Short listening extract about attending events.
Vocabulary bank audio practising festival and environment words.
Sentences with non-defining relative clauses for pitch practice.
Listening and repetition of non-defining relative clauses.

video.summary: Speakers talk about live events and performances they enjoy.

speaking: In groups, plan an eco-friendly festival: name, venue, line-up, atmosphere and sustainability measures, then present it.
Use collaboration phrases such as 'What do you reckon?' and 'Is everyone agreed?' to invite opinions and check agreement.
writing: Write a formal email to a council proposing a sustainable festival, covering purpose, main features, eco-initiatives and closing remarks.
Replace informal phrases with formal ones such as 'Please feel free to contact us'.

practice.q: The festival, ... began in 2003, is one of the UK's best-loved events.
practice.why: Non-defining clauses use which; that is not possible.

practice.q: Fuji Rock reuses wood ... would otherwise go to waste.
practice.why: It refers to a thing and acts as the subject.

practice.q: The venue ... the concert took place was outside the city.
This is the activist ... tent collapsed in the night.

lessons.title: Performers
goals: Learn phrasal verbs for performing and communication
Use cleft sentences to emphasise key information
Reflect on speaking techniques and advise a performer

grammar.title: Cleft sentences
grammar.shortAr: جمل التركيز: It is/was ... who/that و What ... is/was ...
points: A cleft sentence splits one idea into two parts, each with its own verb, to emphasise one element.
It is/was + focused noun + who/that + rest of the sentence emphasises the element after be.
What + subject + verb + is/was emphasises the element after what.
Use the singular verb be after It and What, even with a plural noun.
table: It was a friend who suggested deep breathing.
It was the build-up that scared me most.
What works for me is visualising the audience.
What I needed to do was prepare mentally.
What helped me was the advice, not the practice.
exceptions: Do not use a plural verb after What in this structure.
Use who for people and that for things or circumstances.

vocab.example: She came up with a clever idea for the show.
I was afraid I would mess up my lines.
The concert lived up to our expectations.
Noise from the crowd put me off.
Despite the mistakes, she carried on performing.
Actors put up with noisy audiences.
We ended up laughing about it.
Experience is something to fall back on.
He comes across as very confident on stage.

reading.summary: A social-media thread collects advice about stage fright: performers describe forgetting lines, dealing with hecklers and relying on experience, visualisation and deep breathing.

listening.summary: Podcast extract in which performers share experiences of stage fright and advice.
Listening practice on emphatic stress in cleft sentences.

speaking: Take turns speaking for 30 seconds on everyday topics, then discuss what was difficult and what to improve.
Advise a friend who is nervous about performing, using cleft sentences to focus on the best technique.
writing: Write a short forum reply giving a performer advice, using at least two cleft sentences.
List three ways to cope with stage fright and explain why each one helps.

practice.q: What I needed to do ... prepare both physically and mentally.
practice.why: Singular be follows What in a cleft sentence.

practice.q: It's the character ... matters, not the costume.
practice.why: Emphasis on a thing uses It is ... that.

practice.q: Which phrasal verb means 'to use a plan when other options fail'?
practice.why: It means relying on something as a last resort.

practice.q: The audience's coughing really ... me ... during the solo.

lessons.title: Binge-watch
goals: Use vague language to sound less direct
Recommend a series and discuss viewing habits

grammar.title: Vague language
grammar.shortAr: لغة غامضة: sort of/kind of، around، -ish، and that kind of thing
points: Vague words soften facts when details are uncertain, forgotten or unimportant.
Use thing, bit, stuff and what's her name? instead of precise nouns or names.
Use around, about, -odd or or so for approximate numbers, and -ish for adjectives and ages.
End lists with and stuff, and everything, and so on or and that kind of thing.
table: It's kind of like a detective drama.
The series lasted two days or so.
list + and that kind of thing
I watch crime drama, thrillers and that kind of thing.
exceptions: Use what's his/her name? only when you cannot remember someone's name.

vocab.example: I binge-watched the whole series in one evening.
I watched the film with subtitles.
The cast includes several well-known actors.
I downloaded the soundtrack after watching the film.
The ending has a brilliant twist.
The series is set in Sweden.
The film is based on a true story.
Every episode is incredibly gripping.
The costumes in the series are beautiful.

reading.summary: An infographic gives facts about hours spent binge-watching and related habits; a matching task introduces film vocabulary such as cast, subtitles, soundtrack and plot twists.

listening.summary: Three friends discuss two shows they have binge-watched and what they enjoyed.
Extracts with vague language to complete while listening.
Pronunciation practice on linking and elision in conversation.

speaking: Recommend a film or TV programme to your group and answer questions about plot, cast and setting.
Describe a show with vague language when you do not remember exact details.
writing: Write a short review of a series using film vocabulary and two vague expressions.
Rewrite a direct description so that it sounds more informal and less certain.

practice.q: The show is ... a detective drama, but it's mostly about chess.
practice.why: It makes the description less exact.

practice.q: It took two days ... to finish the series.
practice.why: It follows a number to show the amount is approximate.

practice.q: The film is ... a true story.
practice.why: It means the story comes from real events.

practice.q: The ... was excellent; all the actors gave great performances.
practice.why: The cast is the group of actors in a film.

lessons.title: Music lover?
goals: Learn music genres and interview language
Use do and did for emphasis
Write a forum comment about music preferences

grammar.title: do and did for emphasis
grammar.shortAr: do/does/did للتوكيد في الجمل المثبتة، مع إبراز الفعل المساعد
points: Use do, does or did in affirmative sentences to stress that something is true, often to contrast with another idea.
The auxiliary is stressed in speech: I do like classical music, but I can't stand opera.
Emphatic do can show strong feeling or confirm a belief with a question tag.
After do, does or did, use the base form of the main verb.
table: I do listen to music at home.
She does enjoy playing the piano.
I did enjoy the concert last night.
I don't like jazz, but I do like soul.
You do like this band, don't you?
exceptions: Do not add -s to the main verb after does.
Emphatic do is used in affirmative sentences, not ordinary negatives.

vocab.example: We went to a gig last Friday.
Jazz is my favourite genre.
I like the lyrics and the beat.
The beat makes the song easy to dance to.
She can improvise when she plays the piano.
I enjoy film scores as much as pop songs.
I'm really into hip hop at the moment.
I'm a big fan of live music.
I can't stand opera.

reading.summary: A video-preview page introduces speakers discussing their music tastes and how important music is in their daily lives; a questionnaire asks about instruments, singing and motivation.

listening.summary: Review listening that checks answers to a story about putting on a show.

video.summary: Street interviews ask people about music genres and live performances.

speaking: Ask and answer the music questionnaire, giving reasons with key phrases such as 'I'm a big fan of ...'.
Use do/did to correct a classmate's assumption about your music taste.
writing: Post a forum comment saying what music you like and dislike, using emphatic do or did at least once.
Write three sentences contrasting two genres with do, does or did.

practice.q: I don't like opera, but I ... like classical music.
She ... enjoy playing the drums, although she hates singing.
I ... call them, but they didn't answer.
Which word means a small live concert?
practice.why: A gig is a live performance, often in a small venue.

review.summary: Review of relative clauses, cleft sentences, festival, performance and film vocabulary, and emphasis in a story about an amateur show.
tasks: Combine pairs of sentences with defining or non-defining relative clauses, adding commas where needed.
Rewrite sentences as cleft sentences to change the focus, e.g. 'It was ... who ...'.
Read a story about a community show and choose the best options for grammar and phrasal verbs.

quiz.q: The woman ... I met yesterday is Aki's mother.
This is the pen ... he wrote his books.
The festival, ... began in 2003, attracts huge crowds.
What I'd like to know ... where the ticket went.
It was in 1923 ... the event first took place.
I don't go to gigs, but I ... love live music at home.
There are ... ten episodes in the series.
Which phrasal verb means 'to continue doing something'?
A person who plans a festival is a(n) ...
The ... of the film includes several famous actors.
Which phrase invites another person's opinion when planning a festival?
options: It was the singer who messed up

quiz.q: In 'The show goes on', what did the group initially lack?
Why did the narrator move rehearsals to early morning?
options: Everyone was tired in the evenings
quiz.answer: Everyone was tired in the evenings
